column3: Completes the maternal-protection sequence by showing Moses returned safely to his mother.
Friendship and enmity among the God-conscious do not clarify the revelation to Moses's mother.
Its compact formulation identifies the communication itself as revelation, clarifying the focus's repeated wahy language.
Shows revelation directing Moses himself in a later deliverance, extending the same divine guidance across his life.
Supplies the concealed instruction's concrete content: placing Moses in the ark and water under divine care.
Repeats revelation to a servant while leaving its content unstated, paralleling the focus's emphasis on authorized communication.
The reference to a mother's character does not illuminate divine instruction to Moses's mother.
Casting Pharaoh's forces into the sea forms a distant reversal of the waterborne protection in the focus's sequence.
Shows revelation conveying otherwise unseen narrative knowledge to a messenger.
Shows revealed speech being publicly recited by a messenger after its divine reception.
Directly restates revelation to Moses's mother and adds its protective commands, promise, and future outcome.
Protects revelation's source by denying the messenger authority to alter what he receives.
The unspecified covering of the lote tree adds no clear guidance about the focus.
Places Moses's formation within God's deliberate selection, continuing the providential setting of the focus.
Presents revelation as a true confirming book, adding a scriptural form beyond the focus's private instruction.
Connects reception of revelation with the messenger's defined public warning role.
The casting of fear into enemies is only a remote counterpart to the focus's protected casting scene.
Affirms one divine source communicating by revelation to the present messenger and earlier recipients.
Shows revelation turning prior unknowing into guiding light, clarifying its transformative function.
The extraction of believers supplies only a broad rescue parallel to Moses's protection.
Has God address Moses directly and command attentive reception of what is revealed.
Shows a revealed Quran directed toward warning a community and the final gathering.
Shows the child received within Pharaoh's household, advancing the outcome of the revelation to his mother.
Shows revelation carrying a persistent boundary against associating partners with God.
Defines the messenger by following revelation rather than claiming independent knowledge of outcomes.
Adds the ironic first retrieval of Moses by Pharaoh's household after the mother's obedient casting.
Makes following received revelation an ongoing command rather than an independently produced path.
Places revealed guidance for Muhammad within a continuous commission shared with earlier prophets, including Moses.
Casting truth against falsehood has a different function from the focus's protective instruction.
Pairs revelation to a human messenger with its central proclamation of divine oneness.
Shows revelation giving Moses a practical command for his people's provision.
The identification of one rescued household adds only a general deliverance motif.
Extends divine wahy beyond prophets by making the earth act through an imparted command.
States that the messenger can only follow what is revealed, preserving revelation's source and authority.
A weighty saying cast upon the messenger is a broad communication parallel without the focus's maternal setting.
Joins following revelation to patient endurance while awaiting God's judgment.
Jonah's flight to a laden ship does not clarify the focus's revelation or protection.
The command to seize and bind a condemned person is unrelated to the focus.
Identifies received wisdom as revelation and links it to exclusive devotion to God.
Limits the messenger's knowledge and power to what he is given through revelation.
Receiving a record in the right hand does not add to the focus's communication scene.
Shows revelation remains God's gift and cannot be possessed or controlled by its recipient.
Shows God communicating a directive to angels, broadening the range of revelation's recipients.
Shows revelation giving Moses a concealed night-journey command for the protection of God's servants.
Sets revelation to Muhammad within a long succession of prophets that includes Moses.
Treats inducement to fabricate an alternative as a threat to fidelity to what has been revealed.
The question about worship does not itself clarify the focus's divine instruction.
Describes revelation as transmission of an unseen past event absent from the messenger's direct experience.
The repeated question about worship adds no new connection to the focus.
Shows revelation giving Moses a decisive command in confrontation with falsehood.
The fixed term of a community is unrelated to revelation to Moses's mother.
Commands steadfast holding to what has been revealed.
Shows God inspiring disciples toward faith and public acknowledgment, a different recipient setting for divine guidance.
Presents the revealed Quran as a warning that reaches beyond its first hearers.
The fixed term of a community does not clarify the focus.
Shows revelation answering pressure on messengers with divine assurance and judgment.
A private call to God echoes secrecy but is not revelation or the focus's protective instruction.
Reports revelation about unseen hearers, extending revelation into a narrated chain of reception and response.
God's sheltering of an orphan gives a broad providence parallel but not the focus's communication.
Attributes guidance to what the Lord reveals, rather than to the messenger's own direction.
Mary's withdrawal from her family does not add to the focus.
Marks false claims of revelation as grave wrongdoing, clarifying the importance of authentic divine communication.
Shows revelation to an ordinary human messenger yielding warning and good news.
Requires waiting until revelation is completed, highlighting the recipient's dependence on its divine timing.
States that revelation communicates God's oneness and calls its hearers to submission.
Again links following revealed guidance to exclusive devotion to God.
Shows revelation organizing Moses and Aaron's threatened community around homes, prayer, and encouragement.
Shows received scripture being recited and embodied in prayer, extending revelation into practice.
Shows revelation directing exemplary leaders toward good acts, prayer, almsgiving, and worship.
Divine commands to each heaven broaden wahy's scope but have little bearing on the focus's human scene.
Acknowledges pressure that could make a messenger withhold part of what has been revealed.
Explains revelation as one distinct mode of divine communication alongside speech from behind a veil and angelic mediation.
Provides a contrary model of deceptive whispering, sharpening the distinction from God's authentic revelation.
Shows revealed speech delimiting legal rulings, a secondary application of its authority.
Joins Noah's vessel-building to God's watchfulness and revelation, a practical rescue instruction parallel.
Expands the Noah rescue command into detailed revelation-guided construction and preservation.
Again characterizes revelation as knowledge of an unseen event unavailable by direct witness.
Shows revelation protecting Joseph with future assurance while he faces concealment and danger.
The mention of one's mother and father is only lexical overlap.
Sets satanic whispering to allies as a rival, corrupting communication channel against divine guidance.
Links revelation to divine oneness, righteous action, and undivided worship.
Shows revelation giving Noah knowledge of his people's settled rejection and directing his response.
Exclusive devotion and divine guidance are relevant themes but do not address the focus's revelatory event.
The word for mother in an image of the abyss is unrelated to Moses's mother.
The rhetorical question about the Inevitable does not clarify the focus.
The rhetorical question about the Striking Calamity does not clarify the focus.
A later Israelite request to a prophet is too remote from the focus's revelation scene.
The debate over God's life-giving power offers only a broad divine-authority connection.
The resurrection sign concerns divine power but not the focus's revelation or maternal protection.
Shows revelation directing the messenger to follow Abraham's upright way and reject associationism.
The denial of shared worship supports exclusive devotion only indirectly.
Affirming messengerhood gives only a general setting for receiving revelation.
One community and one Lord offer a broad continuity theme without a revelatory connection.
A truthful narrated account and added guidance are only a distant parallel to revealed unseen knowledge.
The marked punishment of wrongdoers does not clarify the focus.
The endurance of earlier messengers and the unchangeability of God's words give only general support for prophetic continuity.
Sincere prayer during sea danger faintly echoes rescue by water but not the focus's divine instruction.
The warning against breaking oaths among communities is unrelated to the focus.
Angels as messengers offer a general communication framework but no specific link to the focus.
The inheritance ruling does not add to the revelation-to-Moses's-mother scene.
Moses and Aaron explicitly report what has been revealed to them, extending the focus from maternal instruction to their own received warning.
Revelation gives Moses the command that opens the sea, making divine instruction directly effect communal rescue.
Shows the emotional cost borne by Moses's mother after acting on the revealed instruction.
Shows Moses's sister following the child at the mother's direction, adding the family's active role in the protective plan.
The child's refusal of other nurses prepares the return promised in the revelation to his mother.
Explicitly fulfills the revelation's promise that Moses would be returned to his mother and her grief relieved.
Shows God sending angels with His command to warn of divine oneness, broadening the mediating form of revelation.
Divine inspiration to the bee shows wahy operating as directed guidance outside prophetic reception.
Defines warning as something delivered through revelation, clarifying the public consequence of received communication.
Explains gradual revelation as strengthening the messenger's heart, adding a temporal discipline to reception.
Names the trustworthy Spirit as the bearer of revealed Quran, adding an explicit transmission agent.
Shows the Quran sent down in stages for measured recitation, complementing the focus's incomplete-content formula.
Identifies Gabriel as bringing the Quran by God's permission, another explicit account of mediated revelation.
Links revealed book and wisdom with knowledge the messenger could not otherwise possess.
Forbids haste in receiving the Quran, reinforcing the recipient's dependence on the divinely governed delivery.
Identifies the Quranic message as carried by a noble messenger, adding another presentation of its conveyance.
The command to read in the Creator's name presents revelation as the beginning of the messenger's commissioned reception.
